text: New Guinea, the world's second-largest island with an area of 785,753 km² (303,381 sq mi), has the third-largest remaining rainforest globally and the highest plant biodiversity of any island. Located in Melanesia in the southwestern Pacific Ocean, it is separated from Australia by the 150-kilometre (81-nautical-mile; 93-mile) wide Torres Strait, though both landmasses lie on the same continental shelf and were united during episodes of low sea level in the Pleistocene glaciations as the combined landmass of Sahul. The island is bordered by the Arafura Sea to the west and the Torres Strait and Coral Sea to the east, and is sometimes considered the easternmost island of the Indonesian archipelago, lying north of Australia's Top End, the Gulf of Carpentaria, and Cape York Peninsula, and west of the Bismarck and Solomon Islands archipelagos. Geologically, New Guinea is part of the same tectonic plate as Australia, and during periods of low sea level, the two shared shorelines now submerged 100 to 140 metres below sea level, forming the Sahul continent, also known as Greater Australia. The two landmasses became separated after the end of the last glacial period when the Torres Strait flooded. Anthropologically, New Guinea is considered part of Melanesia. The island's name was given by Spanish explorer Yñigo Ortiz de Retez in 1545 due to the perceived resemblance of the indigenous peoples to those in the African region of Guinea. The name Papua was used before Western contact; its etymology is unclear, with one theory linking it to the Tidore language, where "papo" (to unite) and "ua" (negation) form "not united," meaning an outlying possession of Tidore. Another theory, proposed by Sollewijn Gelpke in 1993, derives it from the Biak phrase "sup i babwa," meaning "the land below [the sunset]," referring to the Raja Ampat Islands. The Dutch called it Schouten Island, later using it only for islands off the north coast of Papua proper, and referred to the main island as Nieuw Guinea. The name Irian was used in Indonesia, initially proposed in a tribal meeting in Tobati, Jayapura, by Soegoro Atmoprasodjo under governor J. P. van Eechoed, and promoted by Marcus Kaisiepo in 1945, derived from Biak language terms meaning "hot land" or "heated process," symbolizing a new era. The name was politicized by Corinus Krey, Marthen Indey, Silas Papare, and others with the backronym Ikut Republik Indonesia Anti Nederland ("Join the Republic of Indonesia Oppose the Netherlands"), and was used until 2001 when Papua was reinstated for the island and province. The name Irian, originally favored by natives, is now seen as imposed by the Indonesian government. Politically, the eastern half of the island is the mainland of Papua New Guinea, while the western half, known as Western New Guinea, comprises six Indonesian provinces: Papua, Central Papua, Highland Papua, South Papua, Southwest Papua, and West Papua. The two major cities are Port Moresby and Jayapura. The island's shape resembles a bird-of-paradise, with the Bird's Head Peninsula in the northwest (Vogelkop in Dutch, Kepala Burung in Indonesian) and the Bird's Tail Peninsula in the southeast (also known as the Papuan Peninsula). A vast east–west mountain range, the New Guinea Highlands, stretches over 1,600 km (1,000 mi), with many mountains over 4,000 m (13,100 ft), and its highest point, Puncak Jaya, reaches 4,884 m (16,023 ft). The tree line is around 4,000 m (13,100 ft), and the tallest peaks contain equatorial glaciers that have been retreating since at least 1936. Most areas have a warm humid climate with seasonal variation from the northeast monsoon. The island features extensive lowlands with lowland rainforests, wetlands, savanna grasslands, and some of the world's largest mangrove forests, including Lorentz National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The northern lowlands are drained by the Mamberamo River (formed by the confluence of Tariku and Taritatu rivers) and the Sepik, while the southern lowlands are drained by the Digul, Fly, Kikori, and Purari rivers. The Mamberamo is navigable to Marine Falls; the Sepik, 1,100 km from the Victor Emanuel Range to its estuary, is the longest river in New Guinea and navigable for 500 km; the Ramu is 650 km long, with a navigable lower section and a power plant near Kainantu. The Digul, originating from the Star Mountains at 4,700 m, is the largest river in the western part and serves as a main transport route. The Fly, named after an English Royal Fleet ship that first sailed into its mouth in 1845, is 1,050 km long, navigable for 900 km, with a 70 km wide estuary and tidal effects up to 300 km. Strickland, a tributary of the Fly, flows through wild gorges into the Papuan Plain. Fly and Strickland together form the largest river in New Guinea. Rivers flowing into the Gulf of Papua form a single delta complex. The island's rivers are extremely rich in water due to annual rainfall of 2,000–10,000 mm, with the New Guinea River carrying about 1,500 km³/a (48,000 m³/s), and the Fly alone carrying 238 km³/a (7,500 m³/s)—more than all Australian rivers combined. New Guinea is part of the Indo-Australian Archipelago and biogeographically belongs to Australasia, though its flora has more Asian affinities than its fauna, which is predominantly Australian. The island shares a similar animal fauna with Australia, including marsupials like wallabies and possums, and the echidna, with no pre-human indigenous placental mammals except for bats and about 20 indigenous rodent genera; pigs, rats, and the ancestor of the New Guinea singing dog were introduced with human colonization. Humans may have inhabited the island continuously since 50,000 BCE, with first settlement possibly as early as 60,000 years ago, and the Papuans, the majority of the island's peoples, are descended from the earliest inhabitants who arrived during the Last Glacial Period via the Sahul land bridge. Ancestral Austronesian peoples arrived approximately 3,500 years ago from Southeast Asia, possibly originating in Taiwan, colonizing offshore islands like New Ireland and New Britain and coastal areas of the main island. The island is home to nearly a thousand tribal groups and a near-equivalent number of separate languages, making it the most linguistically diverse region in the world. Ethnologue's 14th edition lists 826 languages in Papua New Guinea and 257 in Western New Guinea, totaling 1,073 languages with 12 overlapping, divided into Austronesian and Papuan languages. Warfare influenced the development of men's houses, and pig-based trade and feasts are common traditions. Most Papuan societies practice agriculture supplemented by hunting and gathering. Large areas remain unexplored, with an estimated 44 uncontacted tribal groups in West Papua. Despite covering only 0.5% of Earth's surface (786,000 km²), New Guinea has immense biodiversity, containing between 5 and 10% of the planet's species—similar to the United States or Australia—and a high percentage of endemics, including over 200,000 insect species, 11,000 to 20,000 plant species, and over 650 bird species. Many species share origins with Australia due to their shared geological history. From 1998 to 2008, conservationists identified 1,060 new species, including 218 plants, 43 reptiles, 12 mammals, 580 invertebrates, 134 amphibians, 2 birds, and 71 fish. Between 2011 and 2017, 465 previously undocumented plant species were described. As of 2019, the Indonesian portion of New Guinea and the Maluku Islands had 9,518 vascular plant species, 4,380 of which are endemic. In 2020, a team of 99 experts cataloged 13,634 species representing 1,742 genera and 264 families of vascular plants across New Guinea and its associated islands, making it the world's most floristically diverse island, surpassing Madagascar, Borneo, Java, and the Philippines. Biologically, New Guinea is considered part of Malesia, a floristic region extending from the Malay Peninsula through Indonesia to New Guinea and the East Melanesian islands.

As of 2019, the Indonesian portion of New Guinea and the Maluku Islands is estimated to have 9,518 species of vascular plants, of which 4,380 are endemic. In 2020, an international study by 99 experts cataloged 13,634 species representing 1,742 genera and 264 families of vascular plants for New Guinea and its associated islands (Aru Islands, Bismarck Archipelago, D'Entrecasteaux Islands, Louisiade Archipelago), making it the world's most floristically diverse island, surpassing Madagascar (11,488), Borneo (11,165), Java (4,598), and the Philippines (9,432). Biogeographically, New Guinea is part of Australasia rather than the Indomalayan realm, although its flora has more affinities with Asia than its fauna, which is overwhelmingly Australian. Botanically, New Guinea is considered part of Malesia, a floristic region extending from the Malay Peninsula across Indonesia to New Guinea and the East Melanesian Islands. The flora is a mixture of tropical rainforest species with Asian origins and typical Australasian flora, including conifers like Podocarpus and Araucaria, Agathis, tree ferns, and several species of Eucalyptus. New Guinea has 284 species and six orders of mammals: monotremes, three orders of marsupials, rodents, and bats; 195 of the mammal species (69%) are endemic. It has 578 species of breeding birds, of which 324 are endemic. Frogs are one of the most poorly known vertebrate groups, totaling 282 species, though this number is expected to double or triple once fully documented. The island has rich coral diversity and 1,200 species of fish, with about 600 species of reef-building coral—equal to 75 percent of the world's known total—covering 18 million hectares off a peninsula in northwest New Guinea. As of 2020, the western portion of New Guinea, Papua and West Papua, accounts for 54% of the island's primary forest and about 51% of its total tree cover, according to satellite data. The WWF identifies twelve terrestrial ecoregions in New Guinea, five freshwater ecoregions, and several marine ecoregions bordering the island. Archaeological evidence suggests humans arrived in New Guinea around 60,000 years ago, likely by sea from Southeast Asia during the Last Glacial Period when sea levels were lower. The first inhabitants, ancestors of the Papuan people, adapted to diverse ecologies and developed one of the earliest known agricultural systems, with ancient irrigation systems in the highlands of Papua New Guinea dating back at least 10,000 years and evidence of sugarcane cultivation around 6000 BCE. The highlands' gardens are ancient, intensive permacultures adapted to high rainfall (up to 10,000 mm per year), earthquakes, hilly terrain, and occasional frost, using complex mulches, crop rotations, and terraced irrigation systems; native gardeners are as successful or more so than most scientific farmers, and evidence shows New Guinea gardeners invented crop rotation before European settlers. A unique feature is the silviculture of Casuarina oligodon, a nitrogen-fixing ironwood tree adopted during a period of extreme deforestation. In more recent millennia, Austronesian people migrated to New Guinea from Taiwan via Southeast Asia, bringing skills in ocean navigation and introducing pigs and dogs; they are considered ancestors of most people in insular Southeast Asia and coastal New Guinea. The western part of the island was linked to kingdoms in modern-day Indonesia; the Negarakertagama mentions the regions of Wanin and Sran, identified with the Onin Peninsula and Kowiai, respectively, as part of Majapahit's tributary system. The sultans of Tidore claimed sovereignty over coastal areas and exported resins, spices, slaves, and bird-of-paradise feathers. Periodic conflicts known as 'hongi wars' occurred when rival groups invoked Tidore's name for punitive or competitive actions. Sultan Nuku, a prominent Tidore sultan who rebelled against Dutch colonization in the 1780s, called himself "Sultan of Tidore and Papua" and commanded loyalty from Moluccan and Papuan chiefs, especially in the Raja Ampat Islands, from his base in Gebe. After Tidore's subjugation, much of its claimed western territory came under Dutch rule as part of the Dutch East Indies. The first known European contact was by Portuguese and Spanish sailors in the 16th century: in 1526–27, Jorge de Menezes sighted the western tip and named it ilhas dos Papuas; in 1528, Álvaro de Saavedra recorded the sighting during a return from Tidore; in 1545, Íñigo Ortíz de Retes sailed along the north coast to the Mamberamo River, naming the island 'Nueva Guinea'. The first map of the island was made by F. Hoeiu in 1600, showing it as 'Nova Guinea'. In 1606, Luís Vaz de Torres explored the southern coast from Milne Bay to the Gulf of Papua, naming Orangerie Bay 'Bahía de San Lorenzo' and Basilaki Island 'Tierra de San Buenaventura', claiming both for Spain. On 18 October, his expedition reached the western part of the island and claimed it for the King of Spain. In 1828, the Netherlands formally claimed the western half as Netherlands New Guinea, establishing Fort Du Bus near Lobo, Triton Bay, which was abandoned by 1835. Due to low economic value, the Dutch promoted Tidore as suzerain of Papua; by 1849, Tidore's borders extended near the current Indonesia-Papua New Guinea border through trade agreements and the Uli-Siwa federation of nine. In 1883, following a brief French annexation of New Ireland, the British colony of Queensland annexed southeastern New Guinea, but the UK revoked the claim, and in 1884, Germany claimed northeastern New Guinea as the protectorate of German New Guinea (Kaiser-Wilhelmsland). Dutch government posts were established in 1898 and 1902 at Manokwari, Fak-Fak, and Merauke. German, Dutch, and British colonial administrators each attempted to suppress inter-village warfare and headhunting. On 18 March 1902, the British transferred administrative responsibility over southeastern New Guinea to Australia, which renamed the area "Territory of Papua"; in 1906, all responsibility was transferred to Australia. During World War I, Australian forces seized German New Guinea, which became the Territory of New Guinea under a League of Nations mandate in 1920, and the territories were collectively known as The Territories of Papua and New Guinea until February 1942. Before about 1930, European maps depicted the highlands as uninhabited forests; when first flown over, numerous settlements with agricultural terraces and stockades were observed. On 4 August 1938, Richard Archbold discovered the Grand Valley of the Baliem River, home to 50,000 Stone Age farmers, the Dani, who were the last large society to make first contact with the outside world. In 1930, Michael Lehay encountered an indigenous group in the highlands who initially believed the explorers were spirits of the dead due to local beliefs that a person's skin turns white upon death. In 1942, Netherlands New Guinea and the Australian territories were invaded by Japan; the Netherlands were defeated and did not resist, and the western section was not strategically significant. The Japanese invaded the northern shore of the Australian territories, aiming to move south. The highlands, northern, and eastern parts became key battlefields in the South West Pacific Theatre of World War II, with notable battles at Port Moresby (Battle of the Coral Sea), Milne Bay, and the Kokoda Track. Papuans provided vital support to the Allies by fighting alongside Australian troops and transporting equipment and wounded personnel. Approximately 216,000 Japanese, Australian, and U.S. soldiers, sailors, and airmen died during the New Guinea Campaign. After World War II, the Australian section was known as the Territory of Papua-New Guinea from 1945 to 1949, then as Territory of Papua and New Guinea. While the rest of the Dutch East Indies gained independence as Indonesia on 27 December 1949, the Netherlands regained control of western New Guinea. In the 1950s, the Dutch prepared Netherlands New Guinea for independence, allowing elections in 1959; the partial elected New Guinea Council took office on 5 April 1961 and chose the name West Papua (Papua Barat), along with an emblem, flag, and anthem. On 1 October 1962, after military interventions and negotiations, the Dutch handed over the territory to the United Nations Temporary Executive Authority, which was transferred to Indonesia on 1 May 1963; the territory was renamed West Irian (Irian Barat) and then Irian Jaya. In 1969, under the 1962 New York Agreement, Indonesia organized a referendum called the Act of Free Choice, in which military-selected Papuan tribal elders voted for integration with Indonesia. There has been significant resistance to Indonesian integration and occupation, including civil disobedience such as raising the Morning Star flag and the formation of the Organisasi Papua Merdeka (OPM) in 1965. Amnesty International estimates over 100,000 Papuans, one-sixth of the population, have died due to government-sponsored violence; reports by TRT World and De Gruyter Oldenbourg estimate the number of killed Papuans since the conflict began at roughly 500,000. From 1971, the Australian territory was known as Papua New Guinea. On 16 September 1975, Australia granted full independence to Papua New Guinea. In 2000, Irian Jaya was formally renamed "The Province of Papua," and a Law on Special Autonomy was passed in 2001. The law established a Papuan People's Assembly (MRP) with representatives of different indigenous cultures, empowered to protect Papuan rights, advance women's status, and ease religious tensions, with $266 million in block grants provided in 2004. Indonesian courts blocked further subdivision of Papua; although President Megawati Sukarnoputri created a separate West Papua province in 2003 as a fait accompli, plans for a third province in western New Guinea were blocked by the courts. Critics argue that the Indonesian government has been reluctant to issue implementing regulations, resulting in the failure of special autonomy in Papua. In 2022, the Indonesian government split Papua Province into four provinces: Papua Province (capital Jayapura), South Papua (capital Merauke), Central Papua (capital Nabire), and Highland Papua (capital Jayawijaya). Additionally, Southwest Papua (capital Sorong) was split from West Papua (capital Manokwari). Inter-tribal warfare and animosity between neighboring tribes remain present in New Guinea.
